body.text: There is something unsettling about memory. It gives tangible shape to tragedies that strike unexpectedly. One of the memory’s cruellest tricks is that it turns uncertainty into a story that feels as though it had always been waiting for us. Jean Said Makdisi’s Beirut Fragments presents a memory that does not give war the shape we have come to expect from books about war.

For Makdisi, memory does not mean a clean progression from peace to catastrophe, or any dependable movement toward resolution. Her memory is a blizzard of interruptions: shelling, shortages, journeys that may or may not be possible, children, neighbours, electricity, food, rumours, waiting. Her memory is that of a life that keeps happening while the city shatters: a mix of comedy, of violence and kindness, of courage found apart. The book watches a world collapse while trying to construct the layers of memories and hopes, of tragedy and the fear of that collapse.

Makdisi’s account is especially valuable owing to her position inside Beirut with several overlapping identities. She does not allow any single one of those to consume the narrative but the reminiscences of each of them can be found throughout the length of her storytelling.

Makdisi moved to Beirut in 1972. She remained there with her husband and children through Lebanon’s civil war and the Israeli invasion of 1982. She is not simply an observer of Beirut; she is also a Palestinian, born in Jerusalem, raised partly in Cairo and educated in the US. She had already lived with the peculiar instability of belonging before Beirut became a battlefield. That history matters a lot for a storyteller, but Makdisi’s account does not turn it into a neat explanation of her.
The book opens with the question: “How can I write about Beirut?” followed by “How can I express my strange love for this mutilated city?”
The question goes on to haunt every page of her book.
Beirut Fragments: Bearing Witness to a War
Profile Books
Pages: 272
Price: Rs.499

For Makdisi, Beirut becomes something more complicated: a place she chose, a place she loved, and eventually a place that could no longer guarantee her safety. The book is an answer to her own initial questions—an answer that is not a political treatise, but rather a sensory chronicle of loss and attachment, written by someone trying hard to hold her world from falling apart. For “the young people who have come to maturity in a war and, like all of us, are at once accustomed to it and not”.

War appears not only as explosions and dead bodies but as an inconvenience that slowly becomes the organising principle of existence. Getting across the city becomes an act of calculation. Electricity and water become matters of concern. A trip to buy something, a conversation with a neighbour, sending children somewhere, finding out if somebody is alive—these small things acquire the weight of major events. Those who live in a conflict zone try to convince themselves that they should no longer be surprised by this new principle of existence; yet, each time, they are caught afresh in its trap. Makdisi portrays the destruction of a city not only through its ruins but through the gradual disappearance of the habits that once made the city and its inhabitants recognisable.

That is where the book’s title becomes important. These are fragments because that is how life under prolonged violence is experienced. Memory itself becomes discontinuous. Years of war cannot be made into a smooth unbroken narrative without falsifying them. Makdisi’s method reflects this. One moment we are looking at the physical transformation of Beirut; another brings us into the intimate world of family life. There is political anger, fear, and observations about human behaviour and loss. The account is rough and uneven, rather like the razed neighbourhoods of war-ridden Beirut, with the pieces accumulating rather than resolving.

The book chronicles despondent times, but in doing so it does not give in to despondency. Instead, it embraces life instead of death, and solidarity instead of the division that war causes. The book narrates a life, apparently meaningless, but fraught with meaning: an act of resistance, and a dangerous one at that.
Cartographer of a vanishing world

We are given a war that is intimate. It is lived—not in the halls of power but in the crumbling corridors of apartment buildings and in a mind trying to make sense of the senseless. Makdisi’s voice is that of the ultimate insider-outsider, a cartographer of a vanishing world. She uses ordinary words such as home, fear, identity, violence, memory, exile, and survival to explore what they come to mean during war. And naturally, language becomes the first casualty of conflict.

A few chapters into the book, the accounts feel less like a conventional history and more like a literary meditation on living through crisis: “We went to the church every Sunday, yet the sound of the athan from the minarets was as much a part of my life as the sunset or the very air I breathed.”

Makdisi explores the contradictions within herself. Living in contrapuntal cultures, we grow up in contradictions; the self is not one consistent thing, and truly understanding ourselves means accepting those contradictions.

The book is also striking for what it does not do. Makdisi does not seem interested in making suffering beautiful: “Our horizons have been so narrowed by the war that we suffer a terrible form of claustrophobia.” The war makes the world smaller even when you are not physically imprisoned: confining the imagination and possibilities of life. Makdisi explains it with anger and a little theatricality.

And Beirut itself remains strangely present throughout. Makdisi remembers the city that existed before the war even as she records its destruction. This gives the book an emotional tension that goes beyond nostalgia. The city is neither an innocent paradise nor merely a victim. It contains its own divisions and contradictions. Makdisi’s affection for Beirut does not require her to idealise it.

Perhaps this is why the book still feels uncomfortable rather than simply historical. It was first published in 1990, yet its central question has not aged: what happens to ordinary people when political violence becomes ordinary? Makdisi’s answer is not particularly reassuring. People adapt. They make tea. They queue up. They worry about their children. They become accustomed to things that should never become customary.

Makdisi writes because cities can be destroyed twice: first physically, and then in memory. Her fragments cannot rebuild Beirut. They do something quieter. They prevent the ruined city from becoming a mere photograph.
Khawar Khan Achakzai is a doctor and researcher with a specialisation in Interventional Cardiology. He is a student of Kashmir history, philosophy, and postcolonialism.
